passage: In the Berlin flat Siddiq sat down with his chemistry notes at 6:15 and picked up his phone “just for one message from Ingrid.” The message was two words. Then a friend's video showed up, and then another, each one starting itself as the last one ended. When Siddiq looked up, the window was dark and the clock said 6:58. He couldn't remember deciding to keep watching. His neck was stiff and the chemistry notes lay open at the same page. “Where did forty minutes go?” he said to the empty room. He put the phone face down on the shelf and felt a little foolish and a little stunned.

qa.q: What time did Siddiq sit down with his chemistry notes?
qa.a: Siddiq sat down with his chemistry notes at 6:15.

qa.q: What did Siddiq feel when the clock said 6:58?
qa.a: Siddiq felt stunned and a little foolish: he could not remember deciding to keep watching, and asked where forty minutes went.

qa.q: What could Siddiq change so a quick check does not swallow the hour?
qa.a: Leave the phone in another room during study, and answer messages at a planned break, since the videos start themselves and there is no natural stopping point.

qa.q: How might Ingrid see the two-word message that started it?
qa.a: Ingrid probably thinks it was a quick, harmless message, and does not know it led to forty minutes of videos.

grounding: A teenager picks up the phone for one quick check and surfaces forty minutes later without remembering deciding to.

passage: Evening study hall in the hostel began at seven. Rajni opened the biology book, and at 7:05 took out the phone under the desk “to see the time”. A friend's story led to another, and the warden Jahnavi moved slowly down the rows, checking. The bell at 7:50 made Rajni jump. Fifty minutes gone, and the diagram of the heart was still unlabelled. Rajni had not decided to scroll; it just happened, one swipe at a time, like walking down a slope. Jahnavi paused by the desk, said nothing, and only tapped the book twice. Rajni slid the phone into the bag and zipped it. The bag went under the bed at nine.

qa.q: At what time did the bell ring in the study hall?
qa.a: The bell rang at 7:50.

qa.q: Why did the bell make Rajni jump?
qa.a: Rajni was startled to find fifty minutes gone without having decided to scroll, and probably felt caught and a bit guilty.

qa.q: What could Rajni do before tomorrow's study hall?
qa.a: Leave the phone in the bag under the bed before study hall begins, so the “just to see the time” check cannot start.

qa.q: How might Jahnavi see Rajni's phone use?
qa.a: Jahnavi probably notices quietly and chooses a gentle tap on the book rather than a scolding, hoping Rajni will make the change alone.

grounding: A teenager picks up the phone for a quick check and loses the study hour to a feed with no stopping point.

passage:
Saurabh: "Didi, you said you'd help me with my science chart at eight."
Irawati: "Yes, yes. Just checking one message."
Saurabh: "It's quarter to nine."
Irawati: (looking up) "What? No. I picked it up for one second."
Saurabh: "You've been scrolling. I watched you laugh at, like, twenty videos."
Irawati: "I don't even remember deciding to watch them."
Saurabh: "That's the problem."
Irawati: "Okay. Phone goes on the fridge. Where's your chart?"
Saurabh: "You'll take it back in five minutes."
Irawati: "Then you hold it. If I ask, don't give it."
Saurabh: "Deal." (He puts the phone in his pocket.)
Irawati: "Right. Photosynthesis. Show me."

qa.q: What time had Irawati promised to help with the chart?
qa.a: She said she'd help at eight.

qa.q: How did Irawati feel on seeing it was quarter to nine?
qa.a: She felt shocked and a little embarrassed, not remembering deciding to watch all those videos.

qa.q: What did Irawati do to beat the phone's pull, and why could it work?
qa.a: She gave the phone to Saurabh to hold and told him not to return it, using distance instead of willpower.

qa.q: What is it like for Saurabh to wait for his sister?
qa.a: Saurabh feels let down and frustrated, watching her laugh at videos while his chart waits.

grounding: A dialogue shows a teenager who picks up her phone for one quick check and surfaces forty-five minutes later.

passage: I'm Minakshi, and in Class 11 I did an experiment on myself. My friend Pallavi said I was always on my phone, and I laughed. "I just check it." So she made me note every time I picked it up during a Sunday of studying. I lost count at forty. Worse, one "quick look" at a video at two o'clock ended at three. I didn't remember choosing to keep watching; the next video just started. I felt sick, honestly, and a bit cheated. After that I switched off autoplay and kept the phone in my bag during study hours. It didn't make me perfect. It made stopping possible.

qa.q: At what count did Minakshi lose track?
qa.a: Minakshi lost count at forty.

qa.q: How did Minakshi feel after seeing the numbers?
qa.a: Minakshi felt sick and a bit cheated, realising the videos had carried on without any choice.

qa.q: What changes did Minakshi make, and why do they help?
qa.a: Switching off autoplay and keeping the phone in a bag during study added stopping points, so willpower didn't have to do all the work.

qa.q: How might Pallavi feel about the experiment's result?
qa.a: Pallavi might feel a little vindicated but mostly glad her friend saw the pattern and changed something.

grounding: A teenager looks back on picking up the phone for a quick check and losing an hour without deciding to.

passage:
Coach's note, under-16 football, Thursday.
Imran arrived for evening practice and sat on the bench to change. He took out his phone "for one second". When I blew the whistle for the warm-up, he was still sitting, thumb moving, boots half laced. Twelve minutes had passed. He looked genuinely startled when Arohi tapped his shoulder. Afterwards he said, "I didn't even open anything interesting." I don't think this is laziness; the thing is built to keep him looking. From next week, all phones go in a basket by the gate before practice, mine included. I'll tell the team on Saturday.

qa.q: How many minutes had passed when the warm-up whistle blew?
qa.a: Twelve minutes had passed.

qa.q: What was Imran feeling when Arohi tapped his shoulder?
qa.a: He felt startled and confused, not realising how much time had gone.

qa.q: What does the coach plan, and why is it fairer than scolding?
qa.a: A phone basket by the gate for everyone, including the coach, changes the setting rather than blaming Imran's willpower.

qa.q: How might Arohi see Imran on the bench?
qa.a: Arohi likely saw a teammate lost in his phone and tapped his shoulder to bring him back, perhaps amused or a little worried.

grounding: A coach observes a teenager lose track of time after one quick phone check and changes the setting rather than blaming him.

passage:
Monday night.
6:10 p.m. I sat down with my biology notes. My phone buzzed. I picked it up to check one message from Pankaj about tomorrow's bus.
6:52 p.m. I looked up and I was watching a video of a man making a sword out of nails. Before that, a dog skateboarding. Before that, I don't know. I don't remember deciding to watch any of it. I never even replied to Pankaj.
Forty minutes. Gone. I felt sick and angry at myself. I always say, "Just one check."
Our science teacher said something last week: these apps are designed so there's no stopping point. Nothing tells you "you're done now." It just keeps going.
So maybe this isn't just me being weak. Maybe I'm fighting something built to win.
Tomorrow the phone goes in Mummy's room while I study. If there's a real message, she can shout.
Ritu

qa.q: What was the video about when the narrator looked up?
qa.a: A man making a sword out of nails.

qa.q: How did Ritu feel after losing forty minutes?
qa.a: Ritu felt sick and angry at the lost time, frustrated with the "just one check" habit.

qa.q: What does Ritu plan for tomorrow, and why is it better than willpower?
qa.a: Putting the phone in Mummy's room while studying, because the apps have no stopping points and willpower alone loses to that design.

qa.q: How might Pankaj feel about the unanswered message?
qa.a: Pankaj might feel a bit puzzled or ignored, waiting for a reply about tomorrow's bus.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager who picks up the phone for one quick check and surfaces forty minutes later, realising feeds are built to beat willpower.
